analysis.one_liner: Bans members of Congress and their families from owning or trading individual stocks.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill to ban congressional stock trading has sat in three House committees without action since its August 2025 introduction, with no vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar members of Congress, their spouses, and their dependent children from buying or selling individual stocks, commodities, and futures, and would require them to sell existing holdings or put them in approved blind trusts. It would allow only diversified mutual funds, index ETFs, Treasury bonds, and similar broad holdings. It would also fine members for late trading disclosures and require financial disclosure forms to be searchable and downloadable online. The bill has been referred to three House committees and has received no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters, who currently cannot know whether a lawmaker's vote on a company is shaped by that company's stock in the lawmaker's own portfolio. Members who already avoid individual stocks also gain a clearer set of rules.

how_it_helps.text: Bars members of Congress from purchasing stocks, commodities, and futures starting at enactment, with sales of existing holdings allowed only during a 90-day divestment window [S2].
Requires members and their spouses and dependent children to divest covered investments within 120 days or place them in qualified blind trusts whose trustee must then sell the original assets [S2].
Exempts only diversified mutual funds and ETFs, Treasury securities, and similar broad holdings, so members can still invest but cannot pick individual companies [S2].
Imposes civil penalties on noncompliant members equal to the greater of a month's salary or 10 percent of the value of each noncompliant holding, assessed every 30 days [S2].

Adds a $500 fine for failing to file required transaction reports under the STOCK Act, and requires financial disclosure and transaction reports to be published online in a searchable, downloadable, machine-readable format [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress with individual stock holdings and their families, who would have to sell or blind-trust them and give up the ability to trade on knowledge gained in office. Financial institutions would take on trustee duties.

drawbacks.text: The ban exempts securities issued or traded in connection with a spouse's primary occupation or corporate board service, a carve-out that members could point to when a spouse holds concentrated company stock [S2].

Enforcement rests on the congressional ethics offices themselves to set rules, grant extensions of up to 150 days, and collect penalties, which critics of past STOCK Act enforcement say has historically been lax [S2].
The $500 fine for late transaction reports is small relative to the value of many members' portfolios, and the bill leaves it to ethics offices to write the penalty regulations [S2].

Compliance would impose real administrative and trustee costs on members and financial institutions, and divesting on a fixed clock could force sales at unfavorable times, which is why the bill allows extensions [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — removing the conflict of interest when lawmakers regulate, fund, or investigate companies they personally own — is substantial and directly enforceable. The main weaknesses are the spouse carve-outs and reliance on the same ethics offices that historically enforced the STOCK Act weakly. The bill's design is broadly sound but its effectiveness depends on enforcement the bill cannot fully guarantee.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees in August 2025 and none has acted on it since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on August 5, 2025 by Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi with original cosponsors from both parties, including Reps. Michael Cloud (R-TX), Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY), Joe Neguse (D-CO), Josh Riley (D-NY), and Jen Kiggans (R-VA) [S1, S2].

It was referred that day to the House Administration, Oversight and Government Reform, and Judiciary committees, which is a standard multi-referral; the record shows no markup, hearing, or floor action since [S4].
It has 16 cosponsors, 6 Republicans and 10 Democrats [S3].

Bills referred to several committees must be acted on by at least one of them before they can reach the House floor; when a committee never schedules a markup, the bill simply sits until the two-year Congress expires [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members who trade individual stocks are better off so far: no committee has acted, so the ban has not advanced and the current trading rules remain in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Members who want to keep trading stocks

for.name: Raja Krishnamoorthi
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited original cosponsors from both parties.

for.what_they_did: Added their names as cosponsors, 6 Republicans and 10 Democrats, signaling bipartisan support.

for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors, giving the ban support on both sides of the aisle.

against.name: House committee chairs (House Administration, Oversight, Judiciary)
against.role: Chairs of the three committees of referral
against.what_they_did: Accepted the referrals but the action record shows no markup, hearing, or vote scheduled since August 2025.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Congressional stock-trading bans with broad bipartisan backing have repeatedly stalled without floor votes, and this bill has not been scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: The cosponsor list is 10 Democrats and 6 Republicans, including original cosponsors from both parties; the lack of action sits with committee chairs rather than an opposing partisan bloc.

industries.note: The bill targets officeholders directly: it would strip their ability to trade individual stocks, commodities, and futures and force divestiture or blind trusts. No committee has advanced it, so the status quo of member trading continues.

industries.industry: Diversified mutual fund and index ETF providers
industries.note: The bill explicitly preserves diversified mutual funds and ETFs as the permitted investment vehicles for members, potentially steering congressional money toward broad index funds.

analysis.trajectory: With three committee referrals and no action for months, the bill's most likely path is to sit in committee until the 119th Congress ends in January 2027, as most stock-trading ban bills have in recent Congresses. Advancement would require a committee chair to schedule a markup or leadership to force a floor vote, neither of which the record shows any movement toward.
